references.text: In the parable of the unjust steward, a master entrusts his servants with the management of his resources, just as this master gives ten minas to his ten servants and expects them to manage them faithfully. See [ref:Luk 16:1-2|Luke 16:1-2].

The parable of the talents in [ref:Matt 25:14-18|Matthew 25:14-18] is a parallel story where a master gives talents to his servants and expects a return—the same basic theme as in Luke's parable of the minas.
The settlement with the servants in [ref:Matt 25:19-30|Matthew 25:19-30] shows the same principles of accountability and reward/punishment that follow from the command in Luke 19:13.
The direct follow-up in [ref:Luk 19:15-26|Luke 19:15-26] shows the result of the command to trade with the minas—the servants give an account, and the one who did not act faithfully is punished.

Jesus teaches about the faithful and wise steward whom the master puts in charge of his household—faithful management of what has been entrusted is a recurring theme that connects to the command "trade until I come". See [ref:Luk 12:42-44|Luke 12:42-44].

Paul describes believers as stewards of God's mysteries, and it is required that they be faithful—the same principle of faithful management as the command in Luke 19:13. See [ref:1 Kor 4:1-2|1 Corinthians 4:1-2].

Peter urges believers to serve one another with the spiritual gift each has received, as good stewards—this is faithful use of what has been entrusted, cf. the command to trade with the minas. See [ref:1 Pet 4:10|1 Peter 4:10].

Paul encourages Timothy to work diligently so that he may stand approved as a good worker for God—a similar call to faithful service in expectation of the Lord's judgment. See [ref:2 Tim 2:15|2 Timothy 2:15].

The exhortation to buy up the opportune time and make the most of it reflects the same principle as the command "trade until I come"—faithful stewardship in the time before the Lord's return. See [ref:Ef 5:15-16|Ephesians 5:15-16].
